challenges before us.This report contains concrete tracks to decline this ambition in all areas - human, economic, cultural -, with a new approach based on human ties and on exchanges between people.As we are going to have new financial instruments, it is up to you, Madam Commissioner, to seize these proposals and to make them live within the framework of the "Team Europe" program.We will be, I promise you, by your side to carry this ambition.My dear colleagues, Madam Commissioner, let's be proud of the community of destiny that binds us all, we, Africans and Europeans.

Ms. President, Ms. Commissioner, dear colleagues!There would be a lot to say and I would have liked to put my speech aside to respond to the arguments that were exchanged here.But let me reaffirm: the agreement still contains - although Ms. Commissioner, tried to negotiate the great deficits of the era de Gucht or to close the worst uncertainty gaps - serious defects.The logic of special rights for foreign investors remains on the ISDS system despite reforms.The inclusion of negative lists, for the first time for the EU free trade agreements, opens the way for further liberalizations, in all economic sectors, also for small and medium-sized companies.The sophisticated clauses for regulatory cooperation leave the thwarted right to regulates on very thin ice, precisely because Ceta is agreed as a so -called living agreement.So we still live on a construction site, despite seven years of negotiations and 1,600 pages of text.However, since CETA is more than a trade agreement, but also significantly influence, as we will in future also include in terms of climate change and necessary changes in our economy, Industry 4.0, I can only say: It is not capable of consent.

Mr. Chairman!I am glad that the Union has noticed the need for reindustrialization after 20 years of deindustrialization policy.Yesterday in this room we adopted idiotic provisions on environmental protection: the Paris Convention, which will cause that 15 to 20 million people in Europe would lose their jobs if, of course, it was done.Fortunately, no one will do it, but here in this room the parliament adopted provisions that will cause loss of work for 15 to 20 million people, due to the increased taxes needed for the idiotic fight against global warming.Well, ladies and gentlemen, this is hypocrisy.I agree with my friend Mélelenchon.However, I remember the times of communism when various workers' delegations were brought to parliaments.The point is not to take care of the rights of individual workers of a individual factory.We must completely change the policy that consisted in the fight against industrialization, with industry, and capitalism.We have to go back to normal.Thank you for your attention.In addition, I think that the European Union must be destroyed.

Mr President, I have served in national parliaments where debates were timetabled to a second and the inability of this Parliament to get its act together means I have to apologise to the Commissioner because I will have to leave before hearing his concluding remarks. The Independent today reported scientist James Lovelock saying that, frankly, it is too late already. The multiplier effect is going to mean that the pace of climate change is going to accelerate and there is little we can do. When you read the European Environment Agency reports that glaciers in Switzerland retreated by 10% in one year alone, in 2003, you think that maybe he has a point, that we are just not realising what is happening. Here we are in this fantastic palace of energy use, debating what might be the end of civilisation. Montreal was a success, but only in relative terms. I am very conscious of the heavy burden you bear, Commissioner. I cannot think of a single person on this planet who has more direct responsibility for coming up with solutions to try and take the world forward, to try and take the economic block and therefore the world with it. You are hemmed in by ridiculous policies – we are still subsidising coal production – and economic priorities come to the fore, as they must, but sometimes to the detriment of the attempts we are all making to try and deal with these problems. So, I urge you, be bold and be ambitious. Let us not pretend that the Emissions Trading Scheme is somehow going to curb aviation emissions to a great extent. We need more measures; we need aviation fuel tax. If we are to deal with car manufacturers, we have got to set mandatory limits on CO2 limits; we have to have smaller cars. It is ridiculous: we are losing the world for the sake of people wanting to drive around in giants. I urge you, Commissioner, take the lead. Governments will always complain and criticise you, but they need you. They will scale back your ambitions, but unless you aim high, you are bound to achieve low.

Today we are talking about the committee's work program.But what really works?Of course, we see Mr. Juncker at work: clearly tipsy kisses and ticks it as if the whole me do not exist.We see Mr Timmermans busy, punishing for the countries that stand up for their own population, such as Poland, Hungary and Slovakia.Mind you, chairman, these are democratically chosen leaders, who are tapped by people here who nobody voted.Nobody.Climate is also such a subject in which the crackle jumps into your glasses when you read it.We go against the global warming with a few thousandths of degrees if we lower CO2 emissions by half.That costs hundreds of billions in tax money.So that doesn't work either.I conclude with the unfortunate plan to work on a European Finance Minister.We see the disastrous consequences of a failing euro in the different countries.By printing 80 billion a month, the currency is artificially supported.That is of course an untenable construction.If the euro has to be on its own again, then hell really breaks loose and the suffering is no longer manageable.So this also works only in the fantasy of the people in the front in the benches.The only thing that really will work is to close this failed experiment and reduce decision -making where it belongs, namely with the democratically chosen parliaments in the Member States.

Mr President, Mr Carlgren, Commissioner, I would like to begin by responding to the previous speech. I do not believe that the European Parliament or the European Union should restrict themselves to modest ambitions in this area. A year ago, we completed the preparation of a climate package which is clearly the most advanced and most ambitious of its kind in the world. We should also acknowledge the fact that it will have perhaps the greatest economic impact of any legislation that has been passed here in the last decade. When I read through the declaration drafted by the European Parliament for Copenhagen, I see things there that I like. The declaration talks of the need to strengthen the role of the European Parliament, of the need to get ready for adaptations to climate change and we can surely all agree with the article on deforestation, in connection with which I would like to stress that deforestation is not, and has not been, a problem just of the developing world, but is also a European problem, so we must focus our attention on it. What is missing, however, is a reference to the need for global agreement, as has been pointed out both by the Council representatives and the Commission representative who is present here. Without a global agreement, we will go nowhere. We talk here about assistance for the poorest countries, which is all very well, but if you look at the current numbers for greenhouse gas production, you can see clearly that even if we were more ambitious in Europe and actually disconnected all of our energy sources, it would not change anything at all in terms of climate change as it is simply impossible for us to slow down this phenomenon. We know there is a need today to talk not only about China, which is repeatedly mentioned, but also about other rapidly developing economies such as Mexico, Brazil, South Africa and particularly India. I cannot imagine what India’s next steps will be and what I have heard so far has not, I must admit, been very pleasing. I would like to emphasise in this Chamber that if we do not reach a global agreement, then all of our efforts will simply amount to a burden on the European economy and a masochistic annihilation of European competitiveness.

Mr. President, Mr. Commissioner, I think it is clear to everyone that we can no longer afford to talk about climate change as a very distant scenario.They are here and hit from all sides, especially in the agricultural sector.In the last two years I have had devastating floods, extreme drought and, earlier this year, a frost that has simply kneeling the vine and fruit sectors in Europe.And let's not forget, that all this came against the background of a sanitary crisis and while the European farmers are preparing for the biggest change in post-industrial history, which comes with a drastic conditions and a low budget.The balance sheet is earthquake.At the end of April, I had tens of thousands of hectares of fruit trees destroyed in eight Member States, but the statistics I refer to does not include all the affected countries, such as Romania, for example.To this balance sheet is added to the vines calamity in a percentage of up to 50%.And when we draw the line, we see that this disaster, which brought farmers to the threshold of despair, will be paid out of the pocket of the four hundred and fifty million European consumers, and this will give an opportunity for importers from third countries who, speculating the moment, will increase agricultural products in their turn.The new common agricultural policy must, therefore, be able to respond promptly to such crises, which are no longer accidental, but become predictable, and the money should not only remain on paper as, unfortunately, it happened in the first year of pandemic.Moreover, climate changes oblige us to adapt the conditions for accessing the crisis fund which, at this moment, cannot be used for frost.In the current climatic context, I do not think we can omit any natural phenomenon from rapid intervention measures.Agriculture is not moft, agriculture is survival.

Angelo Ciocca, in writing.- Negative vote for this report on the Paris agreement in terms of climate change.The Paris agreement is the photocopy of Kyoto's bankruptcy agreement;Both agreements are strongly disadvantaged by industrialized countries and in the absolutely inefficient reality in the fight against climate change.An agreement that masks, behind important issues on the environment, enormous funding to developing countries, such as the Arab oil ones, and which strongly penalizes our companies that will be subject to binding regulations and related charges to promote emerging companies instead of otherscountries, effectively causing a strong unfair competition.

Mrs. President!The basic strategic goals of EU climate policy are quite decent and largely sincerely.However, the tactics used are inadequate.A new climate study proves what we have been seeing for years worldwide: Unfortunately, people act on the basis of short -term incentives, vague prospects for the benefit of future generations, unfortunately, are not sufficient as motivation alone.As a result, we also have to re -align our tactics.We need immediate and short -term incentives to make citizens and companies rethink.Climate -friendly technology as well as basic financial incentives to develop, use and export should put more in the foreground here in this context.In this way, the material profit can become a catalyst of climate change here and now.

Let us not call them earthquakes because they are not. They are tiny tremors, so let us have none of this green nonsense trying to blow things up and create scare stories. In May this year a government-appointed panel said that fracking is safe in the UK and we can move ahead with stricter legislation. In July the Royal Society and the Royal Academy of Engineers also said that it will not contaminate water supplies, so there is an answer straight to your question. Let us not get caught up in green scare stories, because you have driven this debate on man-made climate change for too long with these scare stories and your green agenda.

NATO cooperation in the context of transatlantic relations could not be timely. Europe and North America face multiple common threats – threats to our democracies, climate change, pandemics, terrorism as well as challenges linked to cyber and hybrid threats. I would like to underline also information manipulation and coordinated disinformation campaigns, on which am preparing the report for the Special Committee on Foreign Interference in all Democratic Processes in the European Union. All These challenges require a united and cooperative transatlantic approach bringing together our institutions and Members. A truly strategic EU-NATO partnership is essential to pool our strengths and foster our shared resilience. It is particularly important for Latvia and other Baltic states, which are facing the hybrid warfare, directed by revisionist Russia. Therefore, I fully welcome the call of the report for much more enhanced and strategic cooperation across Euro-Atlantic space. However, the transatlantic community can only protect its citizens if we live up to commitments and ensure adequate resources to deal with the known challenges. I also believe that the military competencies of NATO and the EU and expertise are complementary to address common challenges.

Dear President, Dear and very valued Mrs. Lagarde, Dear Mr. Dombrovski, dear spectators at the screens at home.The annual ECB report is still very sensitive and should be viewed and processed scientifically.The independence of the ECB is the pillar of our common currency in the European Union.The ECB's report should not be a dream concert of this house, because in the end our currency is in international competition with other currencies and also with metals.As a control organ, however, we as a European Parliament have the task of looking at exactly it.I am pleased that in this report we see on both sides what to do.On the one hand, we look critically on the target side-I think that's very good and very right.And on the other hand, something new: do we accept climate change, and will climate change ultimately also find itself in the mandate of the ECB?What we have to pay attention to is that the ECB does not become the second European investment bank.That is our job.On the other hand, I am personally pleased that there are also "small topics" in this report, such as the preservation of the cash, or that we do not reduce the exclusion of the money, or that the generation justice in this report is now finally found.It is also important that I hope that in the plenum we will not worsen the report through various applications.In the end, however, I would like to say one thing that is very important to me personally and that is slowly starting to arise in parliament: This is the demand that Member States receive debts at the ECB.Ms. Lagardde, I ask you to sell with all the vehemence: make sure that Member States also repay the debts made by the ECB.Every citizen in the European Union, every citizen in the European Union has to do so.

I voted favorably the report on the establishment of an instrument of funding for development cooperation, whose main objective is the fight against poverty.I consider that the commitment has positive proposals, namely regarding a human rights and sustainable development approach, including support measures to attenuation and adaptation to climate change.

Mr President, before we start to deal with the consequences, it is always advisable to examine the assumptions.In the case of affecting global climate changes, it is primarily to consider whether the goal is achievable.Of the long series of prerequisites, which must raise doubts in critical evaluation, for time reasons, I will mention only one.Can any measures limited to European Union countries lead to positive global consequences?They can't.A reduction in carbon dioxis emissions by 55 %, if the European Union countries nine percent of the formation of nine percent, means a reduction of about 5 %, and in the previous decade by 17 %.Such a reduction is negligible, even if it is achievable.Can Green Deal's measures dramatically damage the economy and social situation of citizens in the European Union?That can and already happens.

Lady President, she wanted to ask Mr. Faria a question, who said the carbon market is the main instrument to combat climate change.I wanted you to give me examples of sites and moments when the carbon market has ever worked to promote, lead to reductions from greenhouse gas emissions.He said here that he failed to give the signal price: that he then tells me at what time, namely the European Union emissions trade regime, at what time did this price provide to reduce carbon emissions.Second question, if it is available from the failure of this mechanism, to consider another type of instruments.

Mr President, I found this discussion fascinating, and arising from it I have just a few questions which the Commissioner may be able to answer, or at least we will get answers in due course. Firstly, what is the likelihood of public acceptability for autonomous vehicles on the roads, especially in the transitional period, when there may be very few initially and then more and more in due course? Secondly, liability in the event of an accident has been mentioned: is it the passenger’s or the owner’s, who may not be a passenger at that particular time? I think that is a very important question which will have to be looked at. We also have the whole question of costs. Is there any idea about how much these vehicles are likely to cost? Will costs be more or less than the vehicles we have now? And, of course, there is the crucial question arising out of COP21 and climate change: will it lead to more or less emissions? That is hugely important.

Madam President, the Paradise Papers, the Panama Papers, LuxLeaks and so on are not just scandals: they are the melting ice cap of our economic system. They are the financial climate change that threatens to drown Europe’s welfare states and fundamental fairness in our societies, and we must not and cannot allow this to go on in secret. The Paradise Papers have exposed a corrupt global elite of companies and individuals who, through tax havens, write their own tax laws, their own tax rates, as a result of a sick and greedy form of capitalism that has been allowed to run amok. It forces countries into a never-ending race to the bottom on tax rates and, sadly, we know that some Member State governments contribute to this by stalling and diluting new anti—tax evasion initiatives. They do so because the Council and the Code of Conduct Group operates on the principle of unanimity and also confidentiality. This secrecy allows the global elite to deposit their fortunes in tax havens and leaves ordinary citizens to pay the bill. This must change. We urgently need reform of the Council and its secretive way of working on this issue. The people of Europe need to see transparency, and we in the S&D Group also call for a full public investigation into this new scandal. We urge all other groups to join us in a special committee to look into the Paradise Papers and put the spotlight on what is going on.

Mr President, I recognise and fully support all initiatives that aim at improving air quality and life for European citizens. However, I strongly oppose the content of Ms Dalli’s report as, in order to combat climate change, it imposes extreme reductions in emissions standards for new cars and new commercial vehicles in Europe. I would like to remind colleagues that EU measures to reduce CO2 emissions, even if fully implemented, would have a trivial effect on the Earth’s climate, and even if they are implemented, it is unlikely that other major emitters such as China and India will follow suit. Several global studies have shown that the costs of implementing policies to mitigate climate change significantly exceed any possible benefit. For this, and several other scientific reasons, my colleagues and I refute anthropogenic climate change, and disagree with the current EU energy and climate policy.

Mr President, I have to commend my good friend Niels Busk for his brave attempt at yet another cod recovery plan. Ever since I was elected in 1999, we have had a cod recovery plan every year. Every cod recovery plan introduces even tougher regulations and even tougher draconian measures. Because we are dealing with a mixed fishery where the cod is caught together with prawns, whiting and haddock, we have all these discard problems that we have just heard Jim Allister talking about. I am afraid that I feel in this case that Mr Busk is emulating his famous Danish forbear, King Canute, who was King of Denmark and England in the 10th century and famously sat on his throne at the seaside and ordered the tide not to come in. Of course, history records that he got very wet and narrowly avoided drowning. Trying to introduce a cod recovery plan – a management plan that will help cod recover – is, in fact, trying to defy nature in the same way. We know that climate change has caused the North Sea to warm up by one and a half degrees and the fighter plankton that the cod larvae feed on have moved hundreds of miles north, which is why most of the big mature cod that we buy in the shops anywhere in Europe comes from around Norway, the Faroes and Iceland. So until the North Sea cools down again, you are not going to see the cod recovering, and all the tough management plans that we want to introduce will not make any difference. I am delighted, in that case, that I have heard the Commissioner this evening say that he accepts my amendment that will at least look at the impact of climate change on cod recovery, as well as looking at the impact on cod predation by seals. We now have 170 000 grey seals in the North Sea, each one eating two tons of fish a year – including a lot of cod – and previously it was not PC to speak about seals in any shape or form. So at least looking at the impact seals have on the cod population is, I think, a very important step this evening. I commend King Canute to the House and hope that his report is accepted.

Mr President, I should like to congratulate the rapporteur, Mrs Lucas, on her well-balanced report. Indeed, we in the Socialist Group in the European Parliament support her on many points – with the exception of the one about creating a separate emissions trading scheme for air transport. From 1990 to 2002, the CO2 emissions from international air traffic that were generated by the 25 EU Member States rose by 60%. In addition, the altitude at which air traffic produces emissions means that their impact on the climate is far greater than their quantity would suggest. Heavy fuel taxation is common practice in Europe, yet almost nowhere in it is aviation fuel taxed. This has a considerable impact on the competitiveness of the other modes of transport. Long-distance rail transport is stagnating. Parliament should give its resounding support to the Commission’s intention of further pursuing the introduction of kerosene taxes, and implementing these as quickly as possible. The EU must take the lead on this and set a good example by taking timely action at regional level. This report does not discuss only the kerosene tax, however, but also the massive distortion of competition caused by tax exemptions on air transport. Rail transport is subject to taxes and to the Emissions Trading Scheme, which entails considerable cost increases for this environmentally friendly mode of transport. Emissions trading is not a replacement for the measures needed to reduce climate change impact, but it has the potential to be, provided it is properly organised. As I have already emphasised, we support the Commission’s proposal to integrate air transport into the existing Emissions Trading Scheme, but we also support paragraph 24, which calls for a pilot phase of a separate scheme covering the period 2008–2012.

I voted in favor since the proposal aims to increase the effectiveness and efficiency of the Life program and to make it more linked to the Union's priorities.The Life program is a means of dealing with the environmental and climatic challenges of European citizens.It is a small, but well -oriented and effective tool tool.Integrated projects are the main innovation introduced by the new program.These ambitious and structured projects have been conceived according to a global environmental approach and are based on the synergy between community budget, national tools and additional funds of the public and private sectors.Their main purpose is to encourage the implementation of environmental and climatic policy by promoting a coordinated, national and private sector mobilization of the countries of the Union towards objectives concerning nature, water, waste, air, mitigation of climate change and adaptation sectors.

Madam President, let us be clear: this biomass thing is driven by the alleged global warming effect of man-derived carbon dioxide emissions. Forget carbon footprints. CO2 is a natural constituent of the atmosphere; it is not some kind of devil potion, as is misleadingly made out in portraying the situation as an ‘Inconvenient Truth’. This hyperactive film is not proof at all; it is not even truth. It is a theory and a very long way from proof. You see, as a chemistry teacher – and I bet there are few of those in this Assembly – I know what it takes to go from hypothesis to theory to chemical law. I do not go by the theatrical or didactic rantings of a US politician on the make. Fortunately, we now have the Manhattan Declaration, released by 500 scientists last week, which says there is no convincing evidence that CO2 from modern industry is causing climate change. It reminds us that the global climate has always changed and always will. Does no one here appreciate that the Earth we know is not in a final state but in continuous dynamic development? To tax us all to achieve the unobtainable and unneeded is political greed. To turn over farmland to produce biofuels when populations are increasing and there is a world shortage of cereals is madness. To grow biofuels by cutting down whole areas of rainforest, burning the timber where it falls to get a few years’ worth of nitrates and then moving on, gang-raping the precious forests, is criminal. So what is causing the current minimal degree of global warming? To paraphrase former President Clinton: it’s the sun, stupid!

Mr President, Mr President-in-Office of the Council, what, in the case of the Summit, would be counted as a success for it, and what as failure? Yesterday, in Brussels, I heard a high-ranking politician say that even a mini-Treaty would be a maxi-success, yet that, of course, is what it cannot be. You are familiar with Parliament’s position, with our unwillingness to accept any reductions in citizens’ rights, in effectiveness, in transparency or in democracy and we do not see why we should accept anything less, for we know from Eurobarometer that the citizens of all 27 Member States want more Europe rather than less. We were very encouraged to hear you say that there was agreement on the essentials. I believe that the Treaty has to become a ‘Treaty plus’. A certain amount has been added to it since 2004, such as, for example, the debate on protection against climate change, and it would be very fine if the protocol that Commissioner Wallström proposed back in the days of Nice, or some similar wording, were now to be incorporated into this Treaty. I also take the view that the public need a declaration on the social nature of Europe. There are great misunderstandings around about the Treaty, as if it were some neo-liberal con-trick; it could have a declaration added to it explaining its benefits and advantages both for the citizen and for Europe. The institutional balance must be maintained. I ask you to take care to attach the same value to the national parliaments while not allowing the Community method to be demolished. The yellow card cannot be turned into a red one; to do so would wreck the Community method and give this House a far less significant role. Moreover, whilst capacity is not dependent on symbols, no convention would ever have had the idea of doing away with them. Even while talking about giving Europe a soul, we are taking away the few visible signs of identification with it, and that is why I believe we have to take up the cudgels for them too. After all, a minority must not be allowed to dictate what the majority may want. I appeal to the German Presidency of the Council to stand firm, for we are behind you and many Member States are alongside you.

President!The internal and external challenges of the EU are high and grow.Nevertheless, we have to confront them with a household that makes up less than 1% of the Union's gross domestic product - 50 times less than what the national governments spend overall.Even if the EU budget were very efficient, it seems difficult to provide results in key areas with these figures such as unemployment, climate change, research, competitiveness, migration or social cohesion.The debate about the next MFR, especially in connection with Brexit, and also the debate about the EU's own funds-set back on the agenda by the Monti report-will be a good opportunity to check how much the politicalWill is to implement wishes and goals into reality through a strengthened EU budget.

President, Mr. Commissioner!The facts about climate change are clear: we no longer have time.That is why it is always disturbing for me to hear that there are also heads of state who believe that we still have time to wait for solutions.The motto is a little: "Let's take a look at, then we'll take a look." Tried Austrians know this serenity, but it is what will lead us directly into the disaster.I am very sorry to just watch when I continued.We need clear measures because there are already enough goals.We need concrete agreements, because airy ambitions also have many.And we need strict deadlines because there is no time to lose.Every fraction more of warming will be reflected in other disasters: heat waves, drought, floods.COP 26 must become a climate policy revolution.It is also important to me to say that politics is responsible for the next generations who come to us, which will hit it much worse and who will probably be unable to do anything.

The European Union must continue to play a very active role in the fight against the world crisis related to the climate, and the new commission must ensure that environmental protection programs and the effects of climate change can benefit from proper funding.In all its efforts, the EU must consider that policies on climate change should be correlated with the measures taken following the Rio Conference and according to the development objectives of the millennium and the agenda for the period after 2015.

Mr. President, honorable colleagues, this debate on the objectives of the United Nations Conference on climate change is likely to be very similar to the "blah blah blah" whose idol Greta has spoken.Your actions on the environment are ineffective and expensive, and I don't say it, we don't say it, but the European Court of Auditors says so, which criticized you for having spent a mountain of money badly.In fact, 135 billion have already been spent and would have had no effect in the fight against climate change.Despite errors and goals out of reach, you want to throw other money from European taxpayers, another 320 billion for the next seven years and a thousand billion for the Green Deal until 2030. Green Utopia is already producing damage in a context of crisis: serious difficultiesTo find energy, lost jobs, relocations, bills and increasing costs for families.Meanwhile, China continues to pollute safely and has even ordered production to the maximum capacity of over 120 coal mines.Europe makes experiments against citizens, making themselves dictate the line by those who do not give up on low cost flights, air conditioning and latest generation mobile phones.The truth is that your Green proposal feeds on catastrophism, but does not offer such a short time solutions, with the risk of condemning us all to a self -inflicted economic regression.In short, we ask for more pragmatism, a global approach, more time and more attention to citizens, rather than Green fashions.

Chairman, it is high time that we started to distinguish between climate change and climate policy.Yes, we see the global temperatures rising and yes, human behavior speeds up this.But the current climate policy is a complete hoax.If you really want to do something about climate change, we are now starting to build nuclear power plants, we are focusing on market -oriented innovation and climate adaptation and we now stop with those arbitrary net objectives that lead us to a central plan economy based on subsidy and debt.This is watermelon politics: green on the outside, red on the inside.I don't blame the left parties.After all, this has been their agenda for decades.But they are center politicians such as you, Mr. Hoekstra, who make this possible every time.You probably also see the protests outside.The voter presents the bill in June.

Mr. President, honorable colleagues, sustainable growth, socio -economic cohesion, security, migration and climate change remain the main priorities of the European Union's budget for 2018. But there are also other aspects to evaluate.For example, I share the increases proposed by the Commission for the "Guarantee for young" initiative, even if still insufficient.This initiative must be further improved and made more efficient, guaranteeing the contribution of a real European added value to the policies for the youth work of the Member States, and not to replace existing national policies.However, the cut to the cosmes program is not acceptable.SMEs play a fundamental role in the creation of jobs, and the adequacy of funding in favor of this category of companies must remain the priority of the European Union budget.Finally, the unprecedented appeal to special tools has shown that the Union's balance sheet had not originally designed to face problems such as the current migratory crisis and refugees.The cuts proposed are not compliant with the commitment taken by the European Union to face the problem of migrants in an efficient and adequate way.

Mr President, although global warming today appears to be an obvious fact, it is still a good idea to verify the analyses that attribute it almost exclusively to greenhouse gases, something that certain scientists dispute on the grounds that there might be other causes. That being said, if it is proven that greenhouse gases are almost exclusively the cause, environmentalists should ask themselves whether they might not have gone too far in their relentless fight against any form of nuclear power, which undoubtedly presents risks, but which does not emit any greenhouse gases. As the Wijkman report proposes, alternative energy sources must be encouraged, particularly solar and geothermal energy. Such heavy restrictions cannot, however, be imposed on European countries alone, when China, the United States and a good many other countries are hugely increasing their CO2 emissions. As for the storage of carbon dioxide, allow me to recommend a natural, efficient and beneficial method, namely reforestation, all the more so because systematic reforestation could be the subject of a wide-ranging international cooperation programme.

Jens Gieseke, in writing.- I support the proposals of the Commission's work program for 2017. These include, among others.The improvement of the working and living conditions of European citizens, the strengthening of the economy and combating unemployment, taking further measures against climate change and a common answer to the challenges of the refugee crisis.Furthermore, fundamental rights and democracy are to be further strengthened and the European monetary union should be completed.

By this resolution the European Parliament could have strengthened the role of Europe in promoting a binding agreement on the climate.But paved with good intentions and incantations on the desire to maintain global warming within the limits of 2 % by 2050, it does not offer any innovative measure.Worse: it is still and always the carbon emission market, which has repeatedly proven its ineffectiveness, which is the cornerstone of its policy.The fight against warming is not a business or competitiveness matter.As long as the European Parliament and the world leaders remain locked in this vision, no fight against global warming will be possible or effective.I vote against.

Ignazio Corrao, in writing.- The GRóbarczyk report frames the macroiniality of the Juncker Commission for an energy union.Within the relationship, diametrically opposite visions are exposed that see on the one hand the forces that deny climate change, the generation with fossils, even highly polluting and unconventional, support large extractive and generation industry.On the other extreme, those who consider energy policy inseparable from the fight against climate change are located, which aim to reduce the impact of energy costs through the circular economy, which see renewable energy as the main objective for the energy transition, whichThey are contrary to nuclear fission and which favor energy efficiency as the first source, reduction of demand, decentralized production and self -consumption.The speaker did not hesitate to use procedural tools very close to incorrectness, and which have been lived with deep bitterness by different political groups.Considering the slightly controversial relationship I decided to vote against.

Madam President, I had the privilege to listen to Bolivia’s President Arce and Colombia’s President Petro at the Cumbre de Los Pueblos in the Parliament in July, coinciding with the EU-CELAC summit. And they made the point that the summit was a dialogue between two very different worlds. For them, they were the governments of the people promoting participative democracy at community level and multi-polarity on the world stage. For them, the crisis of capitalism was showing a way forward. For them, climate change was a living reality, which had completely changed the free market paradigm, and they couldn’t believe that the Europeans were so naive to think that a problem caused by capitalism could be solved by it. President Petro pointed out that for all Europe’s lecturing about human rights, the reality was, and is, that 250 million people cross the dangerous tropical forests of Colombia to reach the US and Europe. But the greatest mass grave isn’t there – it’s in the Mediterranean. They also spelled out that sanctions and embargoes are killing people, they are equivalent of a medieval siege, punishing the people. If we want a partnership with CELAC, we have to lift the sanctions.

The Joint Parliamentary Assembly  of the African, Caribbean and Pacific Group of States  has become increasingly important in the context of global partnerships, as it has been developing in various areas, especially in terms of the institutions and content, and today it encompasses aspects such as aid, economic cooperation, human rights, trade relations between the EU and the six ACP regions, and political dialogue. This broad array of aspects makes ACP-EU cooperation a unique model for this kind of partnership in terms of development. However, it is important that the JPA maintain pressure on the EU Member States to take steps to honour their commitments in order to achieve the Millennium Development Goals, of greater national parliament involvement in country and regional strategy papers and in implementing the European Development Fund, of measures for combating poverty and climate change, and of strict adherence to all aspects of human rights.
